work_order.understanding:
v4 answers the single objection to v3, and the objection is CORRECT on its facts — I reproduced it before touching anything. v3 specified `schedule_occurrence: keep.schedule_occurrence ?? drop.schedule_occurrence` directly beneath `schedule: keep.schedule || drop.schedule`. The two lines test different conditions: the link switches on the truthiness of `keep.schedule`, the stamp on the nullishness of `keep.schedule_occurrence`. I applied v3's exact expression and drove the real mergeTransactions: keep carried `schedule: 'schedule-keep'` with no stamp, drop carried `schedule: 'schedule-drop'` with `schedule_occurrence: '2025-01-20'`. The survivor came back {"schedule":"schedule-keep","schedule_occurrence":20250120} — one schedule's link wearing another schedule's occurrence identity, exactly as the objection said. The objection's downstream claim also holds: a non-null stamp that is not this schedule's next_date fails BOTH arms of getHasTransactionsQuery (packages/loot-core/src/shared/schedules.ts:196-214), so the merge does not merely fail to help drop's schedule, it strips keep's schedule of a match it previously had through the date fallback — re-opening the exact user-visible symptom AC-1 exists to prevent. v3's risks[0] asserted the opposite of what its own code did, which is what made the defect shippable.

The fix is the objection's second, stronger form: hoist the schedule choice into a local and derive the stamp from whichever side supplied it, so the coupling is structural rather than a convention two adjacent lines happen to follow. `const scheduleSource = keep.schedule ? keep : drop;` then both payload fields read `scheduleSource.schedule` / `scheduleSource.schedule_occurrence`. There is now no way to pick one without the other, because there is only one pick. I applied it to BOTH branches (the split branch at merge.ts:165 and the normal branch at merge.ts:176) and re-probed: the fifth case now returns {"schedule":"schedule-keep","schedule_occurrence":null} — keep's link with keep's (absent) stamp, so the date fallback still matches and nothing is stripped.

Everything else in v3 is unchanged and re-verified: the transfer fix passes the value verbatim (I confirmed `?? null` is wrong by probe), the migration still ends 0x3b, and the sibling-write audit still returns exactly four sites that copy a schedule between transactions.

No decisions were recorded for this issue (plan/brief.md records none), so nothing overrides any of this.
work_order.root_cause: `schedule` and `schedule_occurrence` were introduced as a pair by #7, but #7 only ever taught the WRITE that creates a stamped row. Every pre-existing write that copies an existing transaction's schedule onto ANOTHER row was left untouched, so the two fields can drift apart and a row can end up schedule-linked with no occurrence identity — or, as v3's fix would have introduced, linked to one schedule and stamped for another. `db.updateTransaction` drops undefined fields and keeps explicit nulls (conform() at packages/loot-core/src/server/aql/schema-helpers.ts:136, which returns null for an undefined field and the result is .filter(Boolean)-ed away), which is why these paths silently leave the stamp at its existing value instead of erroring.
work_order.approach:
One rule, applied at every place that copies a transaction's schedule onto another row: the occurrence stamp travels with the schedule link, or not at all — and travels with the SIDE that supplied the link.

The word that matters, and the thing v3 got wrong, is *side*. Whichever transaction supplies `schedule` to the survivor must also supply `schedule_occurrence` for that same schedule. Picking each field independently is not a shorthand for the rule; it is a second, conflicting selection rule, and on the one reachable input where the two disagree it produces a row that matches no occurrence at all.

So in merge.ts the choice is hoisted into a single local before the branch, and both payload fields are read off it:

  const scheduleSource = keep.schedule ? keep : drop;

Then both branches carry `schedule: scheduleSource.schedule,` and `schedule_occurrence: scheduleSource.schedule_occurrence,`. This is the objection's preferred form and it is strictly better than `keep.schedule ? keep.schedule_occurrence : drop.schedule_occurrence` written inline twice: with one local there is exactly one place where the side is decided, so the two fields cannot drift apart in a future edit the way two adjacent expressions can. A reviewer should read the replacement of `keep.schedule || drop.schedule` with `scheduleSource.schedule` as deliberate — it is behaviour-identical and it exists only so the stamp has a single source to be read from.

I re-audited every write that propagates `schedule` from one transaction to another. There are exactly four, all in this change: merge.ts:165 (split branch), merge.ts:176 (normal branch), transfer.ts:68 (addTransfer mirror leg), transfer.ts:131 (updateTransfer). Two other sites are deliberately NOT touched: transfer.ts:78/83/84/89 write matchedSchedule back onto the SAME transaction whose stamp is already correct, and forecast/forecast-schedules.ts:273 copies onto a simulated leg that is never persisted.

On updateTransfer I specify `transaction.schedule_occurrence` verbatim rather than `?? null`. I did not take this on trust: I applied `?? null` and re-ran the partial-update probe, and the mirror came back `schedule_occurrence: null` where it had been 20250120 — every partial API update that never mentioned the field would have silently unstamped the mirror.

The migration fix is a one-byte append. Migrations are keyed by filename, not content, so an already-migrated database is unaffected.

No release note: the behaviour this corrects shipped unreleased with #7.

risks: The merge change means a kept row can acquire a stamp it did not have, sourced from the dropped row, and can LOSE a stamp it had. Both are correct, and they are the same rule: the stamp and the schedule link are now read from one local (`scheduleSource`), so whichever side supplied the link supplies its occurrence identity and the two can never disagree. This is the invariant the change must be WRITTEN TO HAVE — it is not a property v3's code already had, and the objection was that v3's risks entry asserted the opposite of what its two lines did. The reason the wrong form matters: a row linked to schedule A and stamped for schedule B's next_date matches NEITHER arm of getHasTransactionsQuery, so it fails both the exact-stamp arm and the null-stamp date fallback, and the occurrence reads as unpaid — AC-1's symptom, reintroduced through the fix itself.

The transfer change means two rows can now match the same occurrence. Every consumer of getHasTransactionsQuery collapses to a Set of schedule ids or a boolean — schedules/app.ts:602, schedules/app.ts:654 and desktop-client/src/hooks/useSchedules.ts:34 — so an additional matching row cannot change any of their outcomes.

The migration's trailing newline is enforced by NOTHING, and no CI check can enforce it. The pre-commit hook runs oxfmt over a glob that excludes .sql (`grep -c sql .nano-staged.json` returns 0), and the obvious remedy — adding `**/*.sql` to that glob — is unavailable because oxfmt does not format .sql, so the entry would be inert and read like enforcement without enforcing anything. Asserted by qa_script step 9(a) and nothing more.

The no-snapshot-churn constraint is likewise not CI-provable: a .snap file IS the expected value, so a PR that edits it can still be green. Enforced by requiring the new transfer cases to assert on db.all rows and by qa_script step 9(b).

forecast/forecast-schedules.ts:273 propagates `schedule` to a simulated transfer leg without a stamp and is deliberately left alone. It is not a write path — the row is never persisted — but a future change that persists forecast rows would have to revisit it.

QA step 9(b) uses `git merge-base HEAD main` rather than a literal ref, because the branch under test may not be called main and QA may be on a detached HEAD. If main does not resolve, the command fails loudly rather than silently diffing against the wrong base — the safe direction.
No new hosts, no network calls, no new dependencies. Nothing in this change touches a forbidden_paths entry: packages/loot-core/migrations/** is not among them, so the migration edit is permitted.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep v3's two independent expressions but change the stamp line to `keep.schedule ? keep.schedule_occurrence : drop.schedule_occurrence` — the objection's first option, correct but written twice.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It fixes the behaviour but leaves the invariant as a convention two adjacent lines have to keep agreeing on, which is exactly what v3 got wrong and what a future edit can silently undo. With a single `scheduleSource` local there is only one place the side is decided, so the two fields cannot drift apart at all. It is also one line shorter overall, since replacing `keep.schedule || drop.schedule` with `scheduleSource.schedule` removes the duplicated `keep || drop` test.

alternatives_considered.approach: Write `schedule_occurrence: scheduleSource.schedule_occurrence` but leave the schedule line as `keep.schedule || drop.schedule`, so the diff touches only what the objection names.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The two lines would then be correct by coincidence rather than by construction — the same arrangement v3 shipped, which is what let the bug through in the first place. Leaving a known-fragile expression one line above its replacement invites the next editor to 'tidy' it back into an independent pick.

Neither survives as an acceptance criterion CI can honestly prove, so both are checked in qa_script instead.

alternatives_considered.approach: Add `**/*.sql` to the oxfmt glob in .nano-staged.json so the pre-commit hook enforces the trailing newline on every future migration — the alternative the plan review explicitly offered.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It does not work. oxfmt does not format .sql: pointed at a directory containing only a .sql file it errors with "Expected at least one target file" and leaves the byte unchanged; under --check against the file it exits 0 having checked nothing. The entry would be a no-op that reads like enforcement — the same false premise, one layer down. It is also a change to every contributor's commit hook, which is a maintainer's call.

alternatives_considered.approach: Clear the stamp whenever the schedule link is cleared (a shared helper, or an invariant enforced in db/aql), rather than copying the stamp at each of the four write paths.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It does not fix finding 1 at all. The merge bug is not a missing clear, it is a missing copy: keep.schedule and drop.schedule are different values and the code already merges them by hand. A guard enforcing 'no stamp without a schedule' would have prevented neither the merge nor the transfer mirror leg — and it would not have caught the defect this plan corrects either, since v3's failure produced a stamp WITH a schedule.

alternatives_considered.approach: Stop propagating `schedule` to the transfer mirror leg altogether, so a mirror row is never schedule-linked.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: A behaviour change well beyond what the review asked for, in a path (#7) that is already shipped and would alter the mirror's rule resolution and the Schedules page. The reviewer explicitly asked for the stamp to be carried and measured the current behaviour as inert.

alternatives_considered.approach: Drop finding 1 as 'pre-existing, inherited rather than introduced' and file it separately.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The review's own reasoning rejects this: the stamp design is unreleased, the defect exists only because of the new column, and it defeats the central guarantee of the change it belongs to. Splitting it would ship the feature with a known hole in it.

alternatives_considered.approach: Write `schedule_occurrence: keep.schedule_occurrence || drop.schedule_occurrence` to match the `||` style of the line above.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The operator is not the problem — the CONDITION is. `||` and `??` agree on every reachable value (a stamp is a positive YYYYMMDD integer or null, so 0 and '' cannot occur), which is why swapping one for the other would have left the defect in place and looked like a fix. The defect is that the stamp's condition is the stamp's own nullishness rather than the schedule's presence. No operator choice addresses it; only deriving both fields from one pick does.

assumptions: `schedule_occurrence` can only ever be null or a positive YYYYMMDD integer (the migration declares it INTEGER and #7 writes schedule.next_date through it), so there is no falsy-but-valid stamp and the hoisted ternary needs no extra guard.

`keep.schedule ? keep : drop` is behaviour-identical to the `keep.schedule || drop.schedule` it replaces, so no merge outcome changes except that the stamp now accompanies the link. When keep has a link, scheduleSource is keep; when it does not, scheduleSource is drop and `scheduleSource.schedule` is `drop.schedule` — the same value the old expression produced.

The desktop client sends a whole transaction entity on edit, so transaction.schedule_occurrence is present when the UI updates a schedule-posted transaction. This is why updateTransfer can pass the value through verbatim; a caller that sends only `{ id, notes }` leaves the mirror's stamp alone — the intended-and-safe direction, verified by probe rather than assumed.

db.getTransaction returns rows read back through the AQL schema, so keep.schedule_occurrence / drop.schedule_occurrence are null rather than undefined for an unstamped row — either way the ternary treats them the same.

`date` on a db.insertTransaction call is a plain 'YYYY-MM-DD' string and `schedule_occurrence` likewise, not an integer. Both throw `Invalid date` from convertInputType if passed as an integer or a toDateRepr value; I hit this twice while probing and the affected tests[] entries name it.
unknowns: I could not exercise the browser path in qa_script — this checkout has no running app and QA drives that. Steps 2-5 are written from the code, not from a live session.

I verified the merge half with probes and the query half is an existing passing test, but I did not run the two composed together in that file's fixture — they interact through NEXT_DATE and the earlier duplicate's date in a way only the combined case exercises.

Whether any real rule in a user's rule set can assign a different schedule to a transfer mirror leg via runRules. If it can, the mirror would carry a stamp belonging to the main leg's schedule. Already true of the `schedule` field on the same line; recorded as a residual risk rather than adding a condition the review did not ask for.

Whether QA's checkout will resolve a `main` ref for the merge-base in step 9(b). I wrote the command to fail loudly rather than diff the wrong tree, but I cannot know the shape of QA's checkout from here.

Whether the repo would want the migration-newline property enforced by tooling at all. The obvious route cannot do it and the five pre-existing non-compliant migrations are left alone; if a maintainer wants this enforced, the realistic options are a bespoke lint rule or accepting the QA-time check, and that is a maintainer decision rather than this ticket's.
work_order.debate_summary: No council ran on this replan. The decision in front of me was a single objection to v3, and it is correct, so I verified it rather than argued with it: I applied v3's exact two lines and drove the real mergeTransactions, and the survivor came back carrying schedule 'schedule-keep' with schedule_occurrence 20250120 — one schedule's link with another schedule's occurrence identity. The objection's downstream claim also holds on inspection of getHasTransactionsQuery: such a stamp matches neither the exact arm nor the null-stamp date fallback, so the merge would have stripped keep's schedule of a match it previously had and flipped the occurrence back to unpaid, the exact symptom AC-1 exists to prevent. v3's risks[0] asserted the opposite of what its code did, which is what let the defect through review. I took the objection's stronger remedy rather than its inline alternative — hoisting the side into one `scheduleSource` local so the two fields are read from a single pick and cannot drift apart in a future edit — applied it to both branches, and re-probed the objection's fifth case: it now returns null where v3's expression returned 20250120. I added that fifth case to tests[] explicitly so the plan is falsifiable against the code it rejects. Nothing else in v3 changed, but nothing was inherited on trust either: the transfer fix was re-probed, and I measured the `?? null` variant v3 warns against and watched the mirror's stamp go to null on a partial update. Four of my own probes were wrong on first attempt and each is written into tests[] as a named trap, because in every case the naive test would have passed while proving nothing or thrown before asserting — most importantly reading a db.all row as a 'YYYY-MM-DD' string when the raw column is the integer 20250120, and omitting the transfer_acct = 'one' payee, which makes addTransfer throw on a destructured null. The tree is reverted clean; only untracked plan/ remains.
residual_risks: In addTransfer, runRules may assign a different schedule to the mirror leg than the main leg's (`matchedSchedule = schedule ?? transaction.schedule`). The stamp is copied unconditionally alongside it, so in that (unverified) case the mirror would carry a schedule and a stamp belonging to different schedules — the same shape of defect this plan corrects in merge, one path over. It is pre-existing behaviour of the `schedule` field on the same object, so the stamp copy neither introduces nor worsens it, but if it is reachable the guard belongs on both fields together and should cover both write paths.

The migration's trailing newline and the no-snapshot-churn constraint are enforced at QA time by commands, not by CI. A future change could reintroduce either without any test failing. This is a deliberate trade — no test can prove a file's last byte or that a .snap file was untouched, and the one automated route for the former is demonstrably unavailable — but it does mean those two guarantees are only as good as whoever runs qa_script step 9.

The new test cases raise the node suite's pass count above what any earlier note recorded. Nothing in the pipeline pins a count, but a human comparing a CI run against an older plan should expect the number to have moved and should read exit code rather than a total.
